query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A combined experimental–simulation framework that explicitly separates phonon and electron heat transport in defect-containing HfNbTaTiZr (including ~1 wt.% oxygen) will predict total thermal conductivity from 100–1200 K within ±15% of measured values, outperforming traditional single-parameter or perfect-crystal models.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples, some with ~1 wt.% intentional oxygen doping, prepared as polycrystalline bulk to match available experimental conditions and mimic realistic defect content.
generation.intervention: Develop a comprehensive transport model that couples advanced ab initio phonon/electron calculations with separate lattice and electronic conductivity measurements, accounting for real defect configurations using integrated experiments and simulations.
generation.conditions: Validate predictions against measured partial and total thermal conductivities between 100–1200 K using laser-flash or similar high-precision methods for thermal diffusivity, independent measurements of electrical resistivity, and structural/chemical characterization of the doped samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Oxygen incorporation and chemical disorder in the multicomponent BCC lattice, which strongly modifies phonon scattering channels and electronic states, necessitating explicit decoupling of conduction mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By accounting for local chemical fluctuations, lattice distortions, and defect scattering separately for phonons and electrons, the new approach captures cross-interactions missed by standard treatments based on single Debye temperatures or perfect-crystal assumptions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved predictive accuracy by at least 10–15% over earlier models in matching the measured partial and total thermal conductivities across the full temperature range, including consistent partitioning into lattice and electronic components.
generation.baseline: Previous simplified or defect-free models predict total thermal conductivities of ~10–17 W/(m·K) between 300–1200 K without fully resolving phonon and electron contributions or doping effects.
generation.boundary: Applicable to single-phase, BCC HfNbTaTiZr up to ~1 wt.% oxygen between 100–1200 K. Predictions may lose fidelity beyond this doping level or above 1200 K, where additional phases or transport mechanisms could emerge.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative partitioning of phonon/electron contributions above 1200 K is unclear, and further doping (beyond ~1 wt.% oxygen) may introduce untested complexities in scattering behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr specimens with controlled oxygen levels (~0.1 wt.% and ~1 wt.%). Measure separate phonon and electron thermal contributions from 100 to 1200 K using an integrated approach (laser-flash diffusivity for lattice conductivity, electrical measurements for electron conductivity, and advanced ab initio simulations with defect incorporation). Compare predicted total and partial conductivities directly with measured values and existing models.
measurements: Thermal diffusivity and specific heat over 100–1200 K (for lattice contribution).
Electrical resistivity at the same temperatures (for electronic contribution).
High-resolution microstructure characterization to confirm defect distributions and single-phase BCC matrix.
Ab initio phonon dispersion and electron transport calculations with doping.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model’s predicted phonon or electron contributions differ by more than ±20% or total conductivity differs by more than ±15% from measured data at any temperature within 100–1200 K for the doped samples, the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide new research avenues for alloy combinations in the periodic table, opening numerous possibilities in novel-alloy applications. However, their electrical characteristics have been relatively underexplored. The challenge in establishing an HEA electrical conductivity model lies in the changes in electronic characteristics caused by lattice distortion and complexity of nanostructures. Here we show a low-frequency electrical conductivity model for the Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEA system. The cocktail effect is found to explain trends in electrical-conductivity changes in HEAs, while the magnitude of the reduction is understood by the calculated plasma frequency, free electron density, and measured relaxation time by terahertz spectroscopy. As a result, the refractory HEA Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 thin film exhibits both high hardness and excellent conductivity. This combination of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 makes it suitable for applications in atomic force microscopy probe coating, significantly improving their wear resistance and atomic-scale image resolution. The transport behavior of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) remains unclear. Here, the authors explore the fundamentals of low-wear

These alloys thus provide an ideal system to systematically study how the type and number of elements affect the transport properties of equiatomic alloys. Electrical and thermal transport data are reported for all of the alloys for temperatures between 4 and 300 K, and ab initio KKR- CPA calculations are performed to investigate the origin of high residual resistivity (ρR, resistivity at 0 K). The Wiedemann-Franz relationship is used to estimate the phonon and electron contributions to the measured total thermal conductivity. In addition, magnetization data are reported for the five alloys with three or more elements from 4 to 300 K using applied fields between 0 and 4 Tesla.

Recently, PbSnTeSe has been experimentally investigated by Fan et al. [] and Raphel et al. [,], who report appreciably similar results for the thermoelectric performance of the material (see below). The modelling of HEAs transport properties constitute a challenge, and both the simulation methods and their derived predictions have to be confronted to experimental data to assess their validity. In this context, we present in this paper for the first time a complete approach that allows one to obtain all the transport coefficients, including the figure of merit, of a high-entropy alloy. The thermoelectric transport properties of the PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been calculated by combining state-of-the-art methods based on the special quasi-random structures approach to generate the HEA structure, the first-principles density-functional theory (DFT), and the Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo theories. First, from the DFT-computed material electronic states, the electronic transport properties (electronic conductivity, Seebeck coefficient and electronic thermal conductivity) were calculated using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation, and the power factor was obtained.
